title: Capacity phased degradation and model-family hedging
body:
Context and goal:

This is a working sketch for a phased, capacity-aware graceful-degradation system that prioritizes user-visible quality while protecting latency SLOs and predictable cost. Unlike a single blunt "fail to fallback" mechanism, we propose a multi-stage degradation strategy that combines:
- model-family hedging (gradual, versioned downgrades within families),
- capacity tiers (reserve, burst, opportunistic), and
- region-aware spill windows (time-bounded cross-region overflow).

Why this approach?
- Many customers need predictable latency and a bounded cost envelope. When capacity is constrained we should avoid catastrophic decisions (e.g., full failover to low-quality model) and instead run controlled, observable degradations that prioritize high-value traffic.
- Different workloads have different tolerance to quality vs latency; a phased approach allows fine-grained policy mapping (by route, token budget, user tier).

Key concepts / vocabulary (brief):
- Hedging chain: an ordered list of model variants from highest-quality/high-cost down to lowest-cost/low-latency. Each step has a target SLO window and acceptance criteria.
- Capacity tier: reserved (guaranteed), base (normal pool), burst (elastic extra), opportunistic (preemptible, cheap).
- Spill window: a bounded time/traffic window where cross-region requests are accepted to avoid rejecting traffic; has explicit latency budget and ttl for reroute records.
- Soft-fail fastpath: return an abbreviated response (e.g., summary or cached result) to preserve latency when decoding would violate SLO.

Phased degradation lifecycle (proposal):
1) Normal routing: route to preferred model variant in-region using reserved/base capacity.
2) Soft hedging (micro-fallbacks): when per-shard queueing or tail latency triggers, route a small percentage (configurable e.g., 5-10%) to the next model in the hedging chain as a canary. Collect output-quality metrics (e.g., prompt-level evals, heuristic delta).
3) Tiered rampdown: if canary indicates acceptable quality and pressure increases, incrementally shift traffic off the preferred variant into lower cost tiers and variants (policy-driven increments every Ns/requests).
4) Regional spillover with spill windows: when local tiers saturated and cross-region capacity is available, enable spill windows for specific routes. Spill windows include circuit-breaker metadata: max extra latency, cost cap, and a TTL so we don't permanently route cross-region.
5) Opportunistic preemption: when cost needs to be minimized aggressively, opportunistic pools are used but only for non-critical routes or for trace-sampled traffic to validate quality.
6) Hard fallback (last resort): reject, return cached, or use a low-cost canned response if no acceptable capacity available while preserving latency SLO.

Routing policy expression model:
- Policies should be declarative and stored in control plane. Example atoms: route.match (route id, user_tier, priority), capacity.match (region, pool_type), hedging.chain (list of model ids with thresholds), spill.window (max_ms_extra, cost_cap, ttl).
- A rule engine compiles policies to flow-level routing decisions and produces per-request scorecards for auditing.
- Policies must include safety knobs: max cross-region percent, per-customer cost caps, and blacklists for routes that must never spill.

Control plane responsibilities:
- Global policy store: central declarative policies with versioning and rollout (canary A/B for policy changes).
- Real-time signals ingestion: per-shard queue depth, tail-latency percentiles, token burn rates, reserved pool occupancy, and cost burn.
- Routing decision service: lightweight deterministic decision API used by the edge to compute candidate variants and allowed tiers. Decisions are cached short-term at edges to avoid control-plane latency amplification.
- Audit and rollback: every policy change and emergency override produces a traceable event with user-visible metrics and an automated rollback trigger if quality regressions exceed thresholds.

Model variant considerations:
- Variant families should be explicitly labeled with capability vectors (latency, cost-per-token, quality-deltas for common evals).
- Maintain small, well-tested downgrade steps: e.g., 13B fp16 -> 13B q4 -> 7B fp16 -> 3B q4. Avoid skipping steps that cause abrupt quality cliffs.
- Quantized variants used as mid-tier to preserve semantic fidelity while reducing cost.

Observability and evaluation:
- Instrument per-step quality telemetry: prompt-level heuristics (e.g., semantic-similarity against reference for canaries), hallucination signals, token-efficiency metrics.
- Correlate degradations with upstream events: infra maintenance, regional instability, or traffic spikes.
- Implement automated regression alerts that tie to policy rollbacks. Keep a "degrade replay" facility for offline evaluation of how a policy would have behaved on recent traffic.

Cost controls and SLO tradeoffs:
- Each route has an SLO profile (latency P50/P95, cost per 1k tokens budget, minimum quality metric). Degradation policies must respect both the cost cap and the minimum quality threshold.
- Reserve a small global emergency budget for essential control traffic and operator-oncall interventions.

Operational playbooks (short):
- Gradual saturation: when queue depth > X and P95 latency creeping up, enable soft hedging at 5% and monitor quality delta for 5 minutes before increasing.
- Region outage: if AZ/region degraded beyond threshold, open spill windows to paired regions with a 300s ttl and strict cost cap.
- Unexpected quality drop: immediately pause hedging chain and revert to last known-good policy; mark the degraded variants as suspect for investigation.

Open questions / risks:
- How to quantify "acceptable" quality delta automatically across arbitrary prompts? We need a lightweight heuristic suite for online checks (embedding-similarity, token-overlap, intent-classifier) but also offline human audits for new variants.
- Control plane performance: decision API must be extremely fast and fault tolerant; design for full-edge cache fallback mode when CP unreachable.
- Billing surprises: cross-region spill increases egress and variable cloud pricing — need per-customer caps + pre-notifications.
- Complexity of policies: too many knobs risks operator errors. Provide curated templates and sensible defaults.

Next steps / action items:
- Prototype a policy DSL and a tiny decision service that supports hedging chains + spill windows (owner: Marco, target: 2025-03-01).
- Build an offline replay tool to simulate phased degradations against recorded traces (owner: Rina).
- Define a 6-variant family for our most common production model (13B/7B/3B combinations and quantized variants) and run blast tests for quality deltas (owner: ML infra / Liam).
- Draft an ops playbook for cross-region spills with billing guardrails and oncall runbooks (owner: Avery).

Notes to reviewers (quick ask):
- Look for gaps in the policy atoms and any surprising edge cases where routing could route customer PII to opportunistic or preemptible pools.
- Suggest simplifications — fewer explicit knobs if we can safely encode defaults per customer tier.

(End of draft)
